I don't know. Maybe it's because I don't like the way it makes me feel. I don't know.

Fear of Change

I'm a creature of habit, which makes it easy for me to go along with the status quo. I'm not one to rock the boat. I'm not one to challenge the system. I'm not one to fight for what I want. Sometimes, I think I'm just too lazy to fight for what I want. Sometimes I think I'm just too lazy to even want what I want.

When I was younger, I was a little bit more willing to go out on a limb and do things that weren't necessarily comfortable. I wasn't exactly a risk taker, but I was willing to push a little bit. I wasn't willing to take huge risks, but I was willing to take moderate risks.

Can I get some advice?

A. There are two separate considerations here: raising capital and structuring the capital-raising program. The two are related, but they are distinct, and you should consider them separately.

Raising capital is a matter of business development. You need to convince people that you are serious, that they will make money, that they will receive timely updates about how the project is going, and that they will be paid first out of any profits. A business plan can help you convince people of these things; it should also help you decide how much to raise and when.

Structuring the capital-raising program is a legal matter. You want to use a method that is legal, efficient and practical. If you are asking people to invest in your real estate development project, then you will probably be talking about securities law.

The Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 govern the offering of securities in the United States. The federal government regulates these activities because it has an interest in making sure that investors are well-informed about the securities they are buying and that securities offerings are not fraudulent.

As it applies to your situation, securities law prohibits you from selling securities to your friends and acquaintances without registering the securities with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and without satisfying certain disclosure requirements. It is illegal for you to sell securities unless you register the offering with the SEC or qualify for an exemption from registration. An exemption would be available if you were raising the money through a private offering to a small number of people, and you would have to disclose material facts about the offering and the real estate project to the people you are selling to.

Another requirement is that you provide the purchasers with a prospectus, a document that describes the offering, its risks and your background. You will need to have an attorney prepare a document called a "statement of information," which is a form of prospectus, and you will need to be sure the statement of information complies with the requirements of the securities law.

If you have less than 35 purchasers, you may be able to qualify for an exemption from the registration and prospectus requirements. The exemption is called Regulation D of the SEC, and you can get the details of it by reading SEC Rule 506.

There are other rules you will have to consider. For example, you will need to consider the consequences of the purchasers' "acquiring beneficial ownership" of securities in your company. That is, you will need to consider the tax consequences of issuing the securities, including any federal, state or local securities taxes. You will need to consider what types of securities you can issue and what rights the purchasers will have in the real estate project. These are just a few of the things you will need to think about.

I don't drink coffee or tea. I'm trying to eat better, with more fruit and less carbohydrates. I'm on a multi-vitamin and a calcium supplement. I'm 5'4" tall and weigh 141 pounds. My thyroid test is normal and I've recently been tested for diabetes. I'm very frustrated that I'm gaining weight and I'm concerned about my hair loss. What should I ask my doctor to test for? The symptoms you are describing are common to many conditions, not just thyroid disease. In fact, I don't think you have enough information to know if you have a thyroid problem or not. I will list some of the most common conditions that I have seen in my patients with similar symptoms.

Thyroid disease: The thyroid is a small gland in the neck. It makes thyroid hormone. When thyroid hormone levels are low, you can feel tired, cold and you can gain weight. Some people notice thinning hair. Your doctor can check your blood to see if you have an underactive thyroid.

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: This is a condition that affects women and can cause irregular or absent periods, excess hair growth on the face and body, weight gain and infertility. It is caused by an abnormality in the way the body responds to the hormone insulin. Insulin helps to control how your cells use the sugar in your diet. Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) don’t respond to insulin. As a result, blood sugar levels can go up, which can increase hunger and lead to weight gain. Treatment of the PCOS is by treating the insulin resistance, which can be done by diet and exercise, medications and sometimes surgery.

Diabetes: Diabetes is a condition that causes your blood sugar levels to go up. Over time, high blood sugar levels can damage the body. Diabetes can cause weight gain, tingling, numbness in the feet, thirst, hunger, frequent infections and fatigue. Your doctor can check your blood sugar levels to see if you have diabetes.

Depression: Depression is a mood disorder that affects how you feel. It is more than just feeling sad or down. It affects your body, thoughts and behaviors. Depression can cause weight gain, fatigue, loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, feeling worthless, insomnia or excessive sleeping, and difficulty concentrating. Your doctor can prescribe medications to help treat depression, but it is important for you to talk with your doctor or other mental health professional about your feelings.

Stress: Stress can cause weight gain, fatigue, headaches, difficulty concentrating and even chest pain. Reducing stress in your life is important, but it may not be easy. Many people find it helpful to learn relaxation techniques, such as yoga, meditation or other activities that help reduce stress.

Sleep apnea: Sleep apnea is a condition where you stop breathing while you sleep. It can cause excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring, forgetfulness, weight gain, fatigue and headaches. Your doctor can check your blood oxygen levels to see if you have sleep apnea. If you do, doctors can prescribe treatments to help you sleep better.

These are just some of the most common conditions that could cause your symptoms. You should talk to your doctor about these and any other symptoms you are having. If you do have a medical condition, your doctor can help you find ways to manage it.

Answer: Yes, you can deduct the cost of operating your home office, including your part of the landlord's insurance, utilities and property taxes. The main qualifications are that you must regularly and exclusively use part of your home for business purposes, and you must have an actual home office.

One of the most interesting rules about home-office deductions is that you can deduct the cost of the portion of your home that is used as a home office. For example, say you have a 1,500-square-foot home and a 100-square-foot home office. You can deduct 100/1,500, or 7%, of your mortgage interest, taxes, insurance, utilities and maintenance for the year. That 7% is applied to the entire cost, including any improvements you made to the home.

Another important qualification is that you can deduct the cost of the portion of the home that is used as a home office. For example, say you have a 1,500-square-foot home and a 100-square-foot home office. You can deduct 100/1,500, or 7%, of your mortgage interest, taxes, insurance, utilities and maintenance for the year. That 7% is applied to the entire cost, including any improvements you made to the home.

You can also deduct the cost of any additional equipment, such as a computer, printer, fax machine and any other equipment used only for your business. You can also deduct 51/2 cents per mile you drive in your car to conduct business. (You can use an actual expense method if you prefer.)

A small-business corporation can deduct these expenses, too. But if you are an individual, you are not allowed to deduct the expenses of a home office unless you itemize your deductions on Schedule A. If you itemize, you can deduct only the part of your home-office expenses that exceed 2% of your adjusted gross income.

If you are a sole proprietor, your business activities must be conducted from your home. If you're a corporation, your business activities do not have to be conducted exclusively from your home, but you must use your home office at least 25% of the time.

For more information on home-office deductions, see IRS Publication 587.

Question: I am a 62-year-old single man who has been working hard for the last 10 years and have built up a nest egg of about $500,000 in IRAs and 401(k) accounts. A friend of mine told me that I should start taking money out of my IRA and put it into a Roth IRA. He said that the Roth IRA is much better than the regular IRA. Is he telling me the truth? -J.R.

Answer: Yes, your friend is telling you the truth. In my opinion, the Roth IRA is one of the best deals ever for investors. And here is why: If you have a traditional IRA or a 401(k) plan, you are taxed on the money you put into the IRA or 401(k) plan, but you get a tax deduction for the money you put in. Once you put the money in, the earnings are tax-deferred.

With a Roth IRA, you are not allowed to deduct the money you put in, but you don't have to pay any taxes on your earnings. In other words, with a Roth IRA, you put in the money with aftertax dollars and never pay taxes on the earnings again. That is a tremendous advantage.

In addition, you can withdraw the money tax-free in retirement. With a traditional IRA, you are taxed when you withdraw the money. That's a big deal. And if you die, your heirs can withdraw the money tax-free, too. If you have a traditional IRA, your heirs will have to pay taxes on the money they inherit.

Roth IRAs also have a lot more flexibility than traditional IRAs. If you are 59 1/2 or older, you can withdraw some of your money without paying any taxes or penalties. You can even withdraw all of it, if you promise not to put it back in for at least five years. You can also use Roth IRAs to fund a special-needs trust for your children or grandchildren, and you can also use a Roth IRA to fund a Roth 401(k).

As you can see, there are many advantages to a Roth IRA. However, there are some drawbacks, too. For 2007, you can contribute only $4,000 to a Roth IRA. Compare that to a traditional IRA, which can allow you to contribute up to $5,000. Also, you cannot deduct the contribution to a Roth IRA.

Here is the bottom line: If you are in the 25% tax bracket or lower, it makes sense to contribute to a Roth IRA. If you are in the 28% tax bracket or higher, you should contribute to a traditional IRA.

You can find a small claims court in your area by calling the small claims court clerk's office. You can find that number in the government section of the telephone directory.

You do not need a lawyer to file in small claims court. Small claims court is a special court designed for people who don't have lawyers. The judge will help everyone involved understand the rules and procedures. You will have to provide evidence and testimony to support your case. The judge will decide who wins. If you lose, you can ask the judge to consider appealing the case to a different court. The appeal will be heard by a three-judge panel called an appellate court.

If you win in small claims court, you can collect the money by either having the other side pay you or by taking the judgment to a sheriff and having him collect the judgment. If the sheriff cannot collect the money, you have the right to have the sheriff put a lien on the other side's real property. The lien will be in place for four years and will have to be paid in full before the property can be sold.

If you do not win in small claims court, you still have the right to appeal. If you do not appeal, the judgment that you lost will be binding against you.

You have 45 days to file your claim in small claims court. This is a time limit that does not begin to run until you are served with a notice of eviction. This deadline is called the "statute of limitations" and it begins to run when you are served with a notice of eviction.

user_prompt: My 3-year-old has started having screaming tantrums in grocery stores. It happens every single time. I've tried ignoring it, giving in, and leaving the store. Nothing works. What else can I try?
response:
—Diane

A: You've tried the big three, Diane. The only thing left to do is to get your kid out of the store as soon as he starts up.

I understand how difficult it is to leave a store once you're already there. But you're not doing your child any favors by staying and allowing him to embarrass himself. When you give in to his tantrum, you're giving him the idea that you think it's okay to throw a tantrum in public. It's not, and you need to teach him that. Leaving when he starts up is the only way you can do that.

As for your question about why he's doing it in the first place, it could be one of two things. The first is that he thinks it gives him more power. When you give in to him, even though you feel like the behavior is out of control, you're still giving him a reward. And when a behavior is rewarded, it's more likely to happen again. So when you give in to him, you're teaching your child that screaming can get him what he wants.

The other possibility is that he's using the screaming as a way to get attention. Kids who don't get enough attention when they're behaving may act up in order to get those much-desired looks of concern from their parents. If that's the case, you need to make sure that he gets enough of your attention when he's being good.

But that doesn't mean you have to ignore him when he's being bad. Kids will act out if they're not getting enough attention, but they'll also act out if they're getting too much attention when they're acting out. So you need to be careful not to spend too much time with him when he's screaming. The more time you spend with him when he's misbehaving, the more your attention will mean to him, and the more he'll want to misbehave in order to get it.

So when he starts up in the store, get him out as soon as you can. Then give him your full attention when he's behaving.

user_prompt: A financial advisor at my bank is recommending I buy a whole life insurance policy. I'm 28, single, no kids, no mortgage. Is this a good idea?
response:
What are the advantages of a whole life policy over a term policy?

Financially Speaking

Dear Financially Speaking,

Your banker is pushing an expensive and unnecessary insurance solution. It's hard to believe a bank would recommend a product that offers no financial advantage over a far less expensive solution -- even an insurance salesman would have a hard time making the case for whole life.

To understand why, let's take a quick look at the different types of insurance available.

Life insurance can be divided into two categories: term and permanent. Term insurance is fairly straightforward -- you purchase a policy that provides a specific amount of coverage for a specific period of time. If you die during that period, your beneficiaries receive the money; if you don't die, your premiums stop and you get nothing in return. It's sort of like renting insurance.

Permanent insurance policies are designed to provide coverage for your entire life. Although there are several types, many are designed to build cash value -- a savings component that accumulates over time. These policies offer a savings component that can be withdrawn (at a penalty) or borrowed against.

The two most common types of permanent insurance are whole life and universal life. Whole life policies are basically term insurance with a savings component called cash value. Universal life offers similar coverage but also allows you to adjust the death benefit and premiums to your changing needs.

Both types of insurance are essentially unnecessary for young people with no dependents, but they both offer the same benefit: a guaranteed death benefit. And that's the problem. Since you are young and single, you don't have any dependents who rely on your income for support. You may be the sole breadwinner today, but your situation could change with marriage, children, or a mortgage.

The truth is, if you die unexpectedly, your loved ones will have insurance, in the form of your life insurance payout. If you die unexpectedly, your income will not be missed.

So why are bankers pushing permanent life insurance? Because it's a great deal for them.

You see, banks make money selling insurance by charging high fees to cover their overhead and profit. In addition, commissions may be as high as 100 percent of the first year's premium. That's a lot of money for the bank, but not so much for you. A $100,000 whole life policy may cost you $700 a year, while the same policy would cost $130 a year if it were term.

In this case, the financial advisor's recommendation is a classic example of selling the sizzle rather than the steak. The benefits of a whole life policy are far outweighed by the costs, especially when you consider that the primary benefits of permanent policies -- tax-free savings and creditor protection -- can be obtained through other vehicles. For example, a tax-sheltered retirement account or a savings account in your name will offer the same creditor protection as cash value, but will also offer tax-free growth.

The bottom line is that you don't need insurance until you have someone who really depends on you. If you're single and have no dependents, you should consider buying no insurance at all. But if you do need insurance, a term policy is far less expensive than a permanent policy and offers the same protection.

For more information, see the article below on choosing life insurance and the article below on the advantages and disadvantages of term insurance over permanent insurance.

Gary Foreman

 'this is my work, this is the work that Bob did, this is the work that John did, this is the work that we did'.

The idea is to have a record of what you did and when you did it, so that you have something to point to if/when someone tries to take credit for it.

It's difficult for a manager to know what work you did if you don't tell them. So you want to make sure you are communicating it to them. As mentioned in your question, you can do it by summarizing it after a meeting, by communicating it one-on-one, and also by keeping your manager informed about your progress via status reports or other project management tools.

You can also get buy-in from your manager that you should be receiving recognition for your work. You can do so by asking for it. As far as techniques go, here are a few more:

  • Be mindful of what you say and do. For example, if you see someone taking credit for your work, make sure you acknowledge it and say that the work was yours. It doesn't have to be a big deal. First of all, you need to decide whether you can take the time off without losing your job. The good news is that most people do recover from back injuries, and you're not likely to suffer permanent damage as long as you're not in excruciating pain. But if you have to lift something heavy or bend over a lot, you should probably stay in bed until you're feeling better.

Doctors can't do much for back pain. They may prescribe anti-inflammatory medications such as aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen. Muscle relaxers and painkillers such as Darvon and codeine may be prescribed, but none of these medications will speed recovery. In fact, some doctors believe that rest itself is overrated as a treatment for back pain. When the back is in pain, it tends to become weaker, less flexible, and more vulnerable to further injury. So some doctors prefer to prescribe physical therapy exercises that will strengthen your back muscles and help you regain flexibility. Physical therapists and chiropractors may also recommend massage and heat treatments.

The most common cause of back injuries is a problem with the lower back, which is made up of the vertebrae, ligaments, muscles, and nerves. The vertebrae, the bony structures that make up the spine, are separated by disks of cartilage that cushion the vertebrae and allow them to move independently. Damage to the vertebrae, disks, ligaments, or muscles can cause pain. Injury to the nerves in the lower back can cause pain in the thighs, hips, and buttocks.

There are several ways in which the lower back can be injured. The most common is the sprain, which involves the stretching or tearing of the ligaments that hold the vertebrae together. A sprain is usually caused by lifting heavy objects or by a sudden twist or fall. A strain is similar to a sprain, but it occurs when the muscles or tendons that support the spine are stretched or torn. Strains are less common, but they happen when you lift something that is too heavy for you. A third type of injury is a herniated disk, which is a "slip disk" that occurs when the cartilage disk between two vertebrae is pushed out of place. A herniated disk may cause severe pain, but it can often be treated without surgery.

Back injuries can also occur as a result of other problems. For example, arthritis, which can cause pain and swelling in the spine, is a common problem in older people. A spinal tumor may cause pain by pressing on the spine, but this is rare. Spondylolisthesis is a condition in which one vertebra slides forward over another, which may occur as a result of trauma or aging. Spondylolisthesis can be painful, but it often causes no symptoms at all. A pinched nerve may also cause pain, but it's usually the result of another disorder, such as arthritis or a herniated disk.

It's important to get enough rest when you have a back injury. Pain medications may help, but they won't speed your recovery. So don't expect to get better overnight. It may take several weeks to recover. Meanwhile, continue to take it easy and try to stay active. If you can, do gentle stretching exercises to keep your muscles flexible. This will help you avoid reinjury. You may also want to try heat therapy. Some doctors recommend heating pads or hot baths, while others believe that cold packs can reduce inflammation and relieve pain.

As your pain subsides, you can begin to do more strenuous exercises. Start by walking or bicycling for short periods of time. If you're not sure whether an exercise is safe, consult your doctor. Finally, if you're still in pain after a few weeks, or if you have any doubt about the severity of your injury, see your doctor for a follow-up examination.
